title: Occasion, composition and publication
short: Whitman's elegy for Lincoln, written in 1865 and published in Sequel to Drum-Taps that autumn.
body: Lincoln was shot on 14 April 1865 and died the next morning; his body was carried by funeral train from Washington to Springfield, Illinois. Whitman, in Brooklyn with his mother when the news came, composed the elegy in the following months; it appeared in Sequel to Drum-Taps (fall 1865), was revised for later editions of Leaves of Grass, and took its final place in the cluster 'Memories of President Lincoln' (1881). The archive text is the late version. Like 'O Captain!', it never names Lincoln. It is generally ranked among the great elegies in English, in the line of Milton's 'Lycidas', Shelley's 'Adonais' and Tennyson's In Memoriam, but it reshapes their conventions.

anchor: In the dooryard fronting an old
title: lilacs in the dooryard
short: Lilacs were in bloom when Lincoln was shot; Whitman said their sight and scent always recalled that day.
body: In his lecture 'Death of Abraham Lincoln' (first delivered 1879) Whitman recalled that where he was staying 'there were many lilacs in full bloom', and that their sight and odour always reminded him of the tragedy. The 'dooryard' is the small yard in front of a farmhouse door; section 3 describes a real-seeming bush by 'white-wash' palings, with heart-shaped leaves and pointed blossoms. The lilac becomes the poem's emblem of love, renewal and the returning spring, and the first of its three symbols.

title: the great star
short: The planet Venus, the evening star, unusually bright in the western sky in spring 1865; it stands for Lincoln.
body: The 'great star' that 'droop'd in the western sky' is Venus, the evening star. In Specimen Days, in an entry of March 1865, Whitman wrote that 'The western star, Venus' had never been so large or so clear, and seemed 'as if it told something'. In 1879 he recalled walking by the Potomac in the spring before Lincoln's murder watching Venus, 'moody as myself', and quoted this poem's section 8. The setting star becomes the dead president, 'my departing comrade'.

anchor: trinity sure to me you bring
title: the trinity
short: Spring brings three things together each year: lilac, star and the thought of the dead man.
body: The 'trinity' is lilac, drooping star and 'thought of him I love', which spring will always bring back together. The word quietly recalls the Christian Trinity, and Lincoln's death fell on Good Friday weekend (he died on Saturday 15 April, the day before Easter), though the poem refuses Christian consolation. Later the hermit thrush joins, and the closing line braids 'Lilac and star and bird'. Many critics treat the interplay of these symbols as the poem's structure.

title: Section 2: conventional lament
short: A burst of exclamations in the traditional elegiac manner, which the rest of the poem moves beyond.
body: Section 2 is the most conventional part of the poem: five lines of apostrophe ('O ... O ...') lamenting the fallen star, the night, the black murk and the 'cruel hands' that hold the speaker powerless. This is the rhetoric of classical and Renaissance elegy, as in the opening of 'Lycidas'. The 'harsh surrounding cloud' introduces the cloud that reappears in sections 6 and 14 as the darkness of national grief. The following sections turn to concrete things, the lilac bush and the bird, and the despairing cry is gradually transformed.

title: breaking the sprig
short: The traditional elegiac gesture of gathering flowers for the dead, here a single lilac sprig.
body: Strewing flowers on the hearse is a convention of pastoral elegy: Milton's 'Lycidas' asks the valleys to bring their flowers to the bier. Whitman's speaker breaks one sprig, which he lays on the coffin at the end of section 6 ('I give you my sprig of lilac'). The inversion of the sentence ('A sprig ... I break') makes the act ceremonial. In section 7 the gesture is multiplied for all the dead.

title: the hermit thrush
short: The hermit thrush, a shy woodland bird with a famously beautiful song; Whitman learned of it from John Burroughs.
body: The bird is the hermit thrush (Catharus guttatus), a reclusive North American thrush that sings at dusk from deep woods. The naturalist John Burroughs, Whitman's friend in Washington from late 1863, heard it in the Catskills in the summer of 1865 and described it to Whitman, giving him, according to the Whitman Archive, the image the elegy needed. The thrush, 'solitary' and 'withdrawn', sings 'by himself', a figure for the poet, and his song will become the 'carol of death' of section 14.

title: song of the bleeding throat
short: The bird sings in pain, like the nightingale of tradition; song is the outlet that keeps it, and the poet, alive.
body: The 'bleeding throat' recalls the nightingale of classical myth, Philomela, whose tongue was cut out and whose song is grief (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6), and the later fancy of the nightingale singing with its breast against a thorn. Whitman makes the American hermit thrush his singer of sorrow. 'Death's outlet song of life' is a paradox: the song is life's response to death, the release without which the singer 'wouldst surely die'. Addressing the bird as 'dear brother', the speaker identifies with it.

anchor: Night and day journeys a coffin
title: the coffin's journey
short: Lincoln's funeral train carried his coffin from Washington to Springfield, 21 April-3 May 1865.
body: Sections 5 and 6 follow the funeral train, which left Washington on 21 April 1865 and reached Springfield, Illinois, on 3 May, travelling some 1,650 miles through cities including Baltimore, Philadelphia, New York, Cleveland, Columbus, Indianapolis and Chicago, with public viewings along the way. Section 5 is one long sentence whose subject and verb ('journeys a coffin') are held back to the end, so the reader travels through the spring landscape before reaching the coffin. Section 6 catalogues the mourning: draped cities, torches, crowds, dirges and tolling bells.

title: grain from its shroud
short: The wheat rising from its 'shroud' in the earth is an image of resurrection set beside the coffin.
body: The spring wheat has 'uprisen' from 'its shroud in the dark-brown fields', each seed having been buried like a body. The image echoes St Paul's figure for resurrection, the seed that must die to live (1 Corinthians 15:36-37), and Christ's 'Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die' (John 12:24). Whitman places this natural renewal along the coffin's path without stating a doctrine: the land's revival accompanies the dead man's burial.

title: inloop'd flags, crape, flambeaus
short: Flags looped up in folds as mourning drapery; 'crape' is black mourning cloth; 'flambeaus' are torches.
body: 'Inloop'd' flags are flags gathered up into loops or festoons, as they were hung for mourning, rather than flying free. The States appear 'as of crape-veil'd women', crape being the black crinkled fabric of mourning dress. 'Flambeaus' (from French flambeau) are flaming torches, carried in the night processions. RPO glosses 'flambeaus' as torches and 'palings' (section 3) as fence pickets.

title: flowers for all the dead
short: The private tribute widens to all coffins and to death itself; compare Virgil's lilies for Marcellus.
body: Section 7, enclosed in parentheses, generalises the gift: 'Nor for you, for one alone', but for all the dead and for 'sane and sacred death'. The armfuls of roses, 'early lilies' and lilac recall Anchises' lament for the young Marcellus in Aeneid 6, 'manibus date lilia plenis' ('give lilies with full hands'), one of the most quoted passages of classical mourning. The parenthesis marks a turn from grief for one man toward an acceptance of death as such, which the carol of section 14 will complete.

anchor: O western orb sailing the heaven
title: the western orb
short: Venus again: the speaker now understands what the star was 'telling' him a month before the murder.
body: Section 8 returns to the star, Venus, and to the weeks before the assassination when the speaker walked at night and felt the star 'had something to tell'. In retrospect its sinking 'full of woe' foreshadowed the death. Whitman quoted the line 'As we walk'd in silence the transparent shadowy night' (slightly altered) in an 1879 diary entry recalling those walks by the Potomac. The long anaphoric 'As ... As ...' sentence ends with the star 'Concluded, dropt in the night, and was gone'.

anchor: Sea-winds blown from east and west
title: sea-winds
short: The poet's 'perfume' for the grave will be the winds of both oceans meeting on the prairies: the whole nation.
body: Section 10 asks how to adorn the grave. The answer is not incense but the winds from the Atlantic and Pacific meeting over the prairies of the Midwest, where Lincoln is buried, mingled with 'the breath of my chant'. The image makes the continent itself the mourner and joins East and West, as the war had preserved North and South. It anticipates the national panoramas of sections 11 and 12.

title: Fourth-month; the pictures
short: 'Fourth-month' is April, in the Quaker style of naming months by number; the 'pictures' are scenes of American life.
body: Instead of hanging the burial chamber with mourning, the speaker will hang it with 'pictures' of growing spring, farms, rivers, cities and workmen going home. 'Fourth-month' is the Quaker way of naming April by number rather than a pagan name; Whitman had Quaker connections through his family and admired the Quaker preacher Elias Hicks, and he uses such forms elsewhere. The catalogue of sections 11 and 12, with 'My own Manhattan', 'Ohio's shores and flashing Missouri' and the prairies, is Whitman's characteristic method, here offered as a memorial to the man who held the land together.

title: the cloud and the black trail
short: In the midst of busy spring life, the news of death falls like a black cloud over everything.
body: Section 14 opens with a long catalogue of ordinary life, farmers, ships, households 'with its meals and minutia of daily usages', and then 'Appear'd the cloud, appear'd the long black trail' falling 'upon them all'. The cloud recalls section 2's 'harsh surrounding cloud' and section 6's 'great cloud darkening the land': the news of the assassination spreading over the country. From it comes 'the sacred knowledge of death'.

title: comrades three
short: The knowledge of death and the thought of death walk with the speaker like two companions holding his hands.
body: The speaker flees to the swamp with 'the knowledge of death' on one side and 'the thought of death' on the other, holding their hands like comrades. The bird receives 'us comrades three'. The personification is distinctive: death is not an enemy but companionship, and 'comrade' is one of Whitman's key words for male friendship and solidarity (compare the 'Calamus' poems). The three walk together through the remaining sections until he unlooses their hands in section 16.

anchor: tallied the song of the bird
title: tally
short: To correspond or answer: the poet's spirit matches the bird's song as one half of a tally-stick matches the other.
body: A tally was a notched stick split in two, each party keeping a half; the halves 'tallied' when they matched (Latin talea, a cutting or stick). Hence to tally is to correspond or agree. Whitman uses the word repeatedly at the poem's climax: 'the voice of my spirit tallied the song of the bird', 'the tally of my soul', 'the tallying song of my soul'. The poet's song answers and matches the thrush's, so that the carol that follows is both the bird's song and the poet's translation of it.

title: the carol of death
short: The thrush's song, rendered in words: a hymn welcoming death as lovely, soothing and maternal.
body: The 'carol' is the poem's emotional and philosophical centre. It praises 'the fathomless universe' for life and love and then for 'the sure-enwinding arms of cool-enfolding death', which arrives 'to all, to each'. Death is addressed as 'Dark mother', 'strong deliveress', a sea in which the dead are 'Laved in the flood of thy bliss'. The welcoming of death recalls Whitman's 'Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking', where the sea whispers 'death'. The carol has been set by composers, notably in Paul Hindemith's requiem When Lilacs Last in the Door-yard Bloom'd (1946).

title: Dark mother
short: Death imagined as a mother who approaches softly to take her children back; also 'strong deliveress'.
body: Whitman feminises death as a 'Dark mother ... with soft feet', the counterpart to the earth-mother of his other poems, and calls her 'strong deliveress', one who delivers and frees. The maternal figure makes death a return rather than an ending. The speaker claims to offer 'a chant of fullest welcome' that no one has sung before, rejecting the dread of traditional elegy.

title: 'high-spread shy' (textual)
short: A misprint in this transcription: the authorised text reads 'the high-spread sky'.
body: The archive's text reads 'the high-spread shy are fitting', which makes no sense. The 1891-92 Leaves of Grass, the edition this text follows, reads 'the high-spread sky', as in standard editions. The error is an old transcription slip (h for k). Students quoting the line should use 'sky'. The line belongs to the carol's list of the 'serenades' and 'adornments' offered to death: the open landscape, the sky, the fields and the 'huge and thoughtful night', which the speaker presents as fitting gifts.

anchor: And I saw askant the armies
title: the vision of the war dead
short: A sidelong vision of battle-flags and corpses: the dead are at rest; the living suffer.
body: 'Askant' means sideways, obliquely (RPO). The speaker's sight, 'unclosed', sees battle-flags shot through and torn, 'battle-corpses, myriads of them', 'white skeletons of young men'. Whitman had seen the war's wounded closely as a volunteer visitor in Washington hospitals from 1862, recorded in Memoranda During the War and Specimen Days. The vision widens the elegy from Lincoln to the war's hundreds of thousands of dead. Its conclusion reverses expectation: the dead 'suffer'd not'; it is the living, mothers, wives, children, comrades, who suffer.

anchor: Lilac and star and bird twined
title: The ending
short: The three symbols are braided with the poet's song and left 'There in the fragrant pines and the cedars dusk and dim'.
body: Section 16 is a long leave-taking with the participle 'Passing' repeated: the speaker leaves the lilac 'blooming, returning with spring', ceases his song to the star, and lets go his comrades' hands. Yet he will keep everything, 'retrievements out of the night'. The final lines name the dead man's quality most directly, 'the sweetest, wisest soul of all my days and lands', and braid 'Lilac and star and bird' with 'the chant of my soul'. The closing image returns to the swamp's pines and cedars, ending in the bird's dim haunt rather than in heaven.
